strengths: The paper identifies a concrete problem in class–pose decomposition: arbitrary canonical orientations make learned pose distributions difficult to compare. Explicit normalization is a simple, interpretable solution that can reuse existing backbones.

Experiments cover both SO(2) images and SO(3) molecular conformations. The image results show promising recovery of class-dependent rotation ranges, and the molecular experiment demonstrates implementation at substantial scale.
The manuscript provides useful architectural and training details, a neighborhood-size ablation, and an application to OOD pose detection with reported AUROCs of 0.92, 0.80, and 0.75.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees need tighter assumptions. Proposition 3.1 is stated for general Lie groups, but its proof requires a right-invariant metric and invokes local convexity/concentration conditions for stability of the Fréchet mean without establishing them. Broad or symmetric distributions can lack a unique centroid, so the claim that the framework handles any distribution is unsupported. Exact group-valued equivariance also requires addressing objects with nontrivial stabilizers.

The implementation does not consistently match the mathematical method. Appendix C equates the SO(2) circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean, although these generally differ, and uses a fitted matrix-Fisher mode for SO(3) without establishing equivalence to the required mean. The stated scalar coth(s)−1/s inversion is not a general matrix-Fisher concentration estimator. Additionally, Section 3.3 applies ψ(x)Λ(x)⁻¹ to canonicalize x; under the stated reconstruction convention, the required transformation is its inverse, Λ(x)ψ(x)⁻¹.

The claimed resolution of the 6-versus-9 ambiguity is not established. If two inputs are exactly rotation-related, the invariant encoder and invariant offset predictor must give identical outputs, preventing separate class-dependent normalization. Handwriting differences could explain the illustrated separation, but this would not demonstrate that RECON overcomes the inherent ambiguity of full rotational invariance.

There are no quantitative comparisons against SGM, the closely related symmetry-discovery method [42], or simple centered pose-estimation baselines. Qualitative comparisons with unnormalized canonicals do not establish a competitive advance. In particular, centering an SGM distribution and evaluating its likelihood would be an important comparison; coordinate normalization alone does not improve likelihood-based OOD discrimination when performed consistently.

The molecular accuracy criterion is inadequately justified. The claim that approximately 80% of molecules are accurately predicted uses MSE < 800 based on visual inspection. Under ordinary elementwise matrix MSE, the constant predictor F = 33.334 I scores approximately 741 against every one of the three target matrices, satisfying that threshold without identifying the rotation axis. Distributional metrics, aggregate errors, and this trivial baseline are needed.

Experimental scope is narrower than the claims suggest. Molecular orientations are synthetically sampled from only three prescribed distributions after reference alignment, and train/test splits contain conformers of the same molecules. This tests recovery of imposed pose distributions for known molecular identities, not discovery of naturally occurring symmetries or generalization to unseen molecules. Multimodal distributions and substantial structural deviations are not evaluated.

Robustness and reproducibility evidence remain incomplete: experiments use one fixed seed, the moment-based image estimators are not fully specified, and neighborhood purity is not measured. The fixed-k neighborhood approximation is also not covered by the theorem's growing-sample guarantee. These gaps, together with the missing baselines and technical inconsistencies, prevent an acceptance-level assessment.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical issue in class-pose decomposition: arbitrary canonical orientations make pose distributions difficult to compare. Explicit normalization is simple, interpretable, and potentially reusable across backbones.

Experiments cover both SO(2) images and SO(3) molecular conformations. The image results show reasonably accurate recovery of imposed rotation ranges, and the molecular experiments extend the implementation beyond standard image benchmarks.
The appendix provides substantial architecture, preprocessing, and training details. Neighborhood-size sensitivity and an OOD-pose detection application provide useful additional analysis.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantee is insufficiently qualified. Proposition 3.1 is stated for a general Lie group, but its proof requires a right-invariant metric and invokes local convexity and Lipschitz stability of the Fréchet mean without establishing the necessary support conditions. Broad or multimodal distributions can have nonunique or unstable means. These concerns are particularly relevant to the nearly unrestricted rotation around one axis used in the SO(3) experiments; the claim of learning any distribution over a Lie group is unsupported.

The implemented estimators do not clearly match the theory. Appendix C.1 equates the circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean, although these differ in general. Appendix C.2 estimates the SO(3) Fréchet mean using the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution, without proving equivalence or assessing approximation error. Its parameter estimator also uses the scalar relation coth(s)−1/s, whereas general matrix-Fisher moment matching involves coupled derivatives of its normalizing constant. These discrepancies require clarification and numerical validation.

The claimed resolution of rotation-related class ambiguity is inconsistent with the architecture as stated. If a '9' is exactly a rotated '6', their invariant embeddings coincide, so invariant neighborhood selection and invariant offset prediction cannot distinguish them. Actual MNIST digits may differ in shape, but Figure 6b does not establish that RECON overcomes this fundamental ambiguity. Controlled same-orbit examples and neighborhood-purity measurements are needed.

The evaluation lacks quantitative comparisons against the closest alternatives. SGM and IE-AE are compared mainly through canonical visualizations; there are no matched distribution-recovery or OOD benchmarks against SGM, a centered SGM, or simple pose-density estimators. Since consistently translating both a pose and its density preserves likelihood, the reported OOD AUROCs alone do not demonstrate a benefit from canonical normalization. Multiple training seeds and uncertainty estimates are also absent.

The molecular experiment tests a restricted synthetic setting rather than discovery of naturally occurring molecular orientation distributions. Conformers are prealigned using molecule-specific reference structures and assigned one of only three rotation distributions. Training and testing contain the same molecular identities, with distributions assigned randomly by identity. This supports recovery for additional conformers of known molecules, but does not establish generalization to unseen molecular classes or broadly varying symmetry distributions.

The molecular accuracy claims are weakly substantiated. The assertion that approximately 80% of molecules have accurate predictions relies on an MSE threshold selected through visual inspection. Parameter MSE is not directly interpretable as distributional fidelity; held-out likelihood, distribution distances, and simple reference baselines would make the results substantially more convincing. A lack of visible correlation with molecular attributes also does not establish robustness to conformational complexity.

The central contribution is an incremental centering procedure atop an existing decomposition model, and its practical reliability depends on unvalidated neighborhood assumptions. The theorem assumes independent samples from a valid class, whereas the implementation uses 25 nearest neighbors without measuring class contamination or pose-dependent selection. There are also algebraic inconsistencies: Section 3.3 applies ψ(x)Λ(x)⁻¹ to the input for canonicalization, although the stated reconstruction convention requires the inverse transformation, and Appendix C.2 inconsistently writes the normalization without the inverse. Together with the missing comparisons and theoretical qualifications, these issues place the submission below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful ambiguity in class-pose decomposition: arbitrary canonical orientations make pose distributions difficult to compare. Explicit normalization is a simple, interpretable approach to this problem.
Experiments cover both SO(2) images and SO(3) molecular conformations. The canonicalization visualizations, neighborhood-size analysis, and OOD detection results provide useful initial evidence.
The manuscript is generally clear, and the appendix provides substantial architecture, training, preprocessing, and computational-cost details.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee is broader than its justification. Appendix B relies on a right-invariant metric and on concentration within regions where the Fréchet functional is strictly convex and its mean is stable, but these conditions are not specified in Proposition 3.1 or verified experimentally. Broad or nearly rotation-invariant distributions can have nonunique or unstable means; the molecular distributions deliberately allow nearly free rotation around an axis. Consequently, the claimed general recovery guarantee needs tighter assumptions and analysis.

The implemented estimators do not match the theoretical construction. Appendix C.1 identifies the circular mean with the intrinsic Fréchet mean, although they generally differ. Appendix C.2 substitutes a fitted matrix-Fisher mode for the Fréchet mean and describes concentration estimation through independent inversion of coth(s)−1/s; general matrix-Fisher moment equations depend jointly on the singular values. These discrepancies directly affect the central normalization and SO(3) recovery claims and require justification or correction.

The claimed resolution of the ‘6 versus 9’ ambiguity is not established. Exactly rotation-related inputs have identical invariant embeddings, identical invariant neighborhoods, and identical outputs from the invariant offset predictor. Normalization therefore cannot distinguish them using contextual orientation alone. Actual handwritten classes might remain separable through shape differences, but the paper needs neighborhood-purity measurements and controlled examples to distinguish that explanation from its claimed handling of partial symmetry.

Quantitative comparisons are insufficient. SGM and IE-AE are compared mainly through qualitative canonicalizations, without competitive distribution-recovery or OOD baselines. In particular, centering SGM's learned distributions is an essential comparison for establishing the contribution beyond existing decomposition methods. Multiple training seeds, uncertainty estimates, and ablations separating neighborhood estimation, centering, and learned predictors are also missing.

The molecular evaluation supports a narrower conclusion than claimed. Conformers are prealigned to a molecule-specific reference, assigned one of only three synthetic rotation distributions, and split within each molecule, so test molecules are already represented during training. This does not demonstrate discovery of naturally occurring molecular orientation distributions or generalization to unseen molecular identities. Parameter MSE is difficult to interpret without simple baselines or distribution-level metrics, and declaring MSE below approximately 800 accurate based on visualizations is not a convincing quantitative criterion.

There are consequential specification errors and reproducibility gaps. Under the paper's stated action convention, canonicalizing an input requires applying the inverse of its normalized pose, whereas Section 3.3 applies the normalized pose itself. Appendix C.2 also omits the inverse in its normalization expression. The robust moment estimators for images and the exact OOD sampling and labeling protocol are insufficiently specified. These issues prevent confidently connecting the reported results to the proposed algorithm.

strengths: Addresses a concrete limitation of class-pose models: arbitrary canonical orientations can impair interpretation and deployment with frozen classifiers. The proposed normalization is simple and geometrically motivated.
Reports substantial improvements in frozen-classifier accuracy on rotated MNIST (66.90% to 92.94%) and FashionMNIST (57.52% to 80.32%), alongside improved OOD detection.
Extends evaluation to SO(3) molecular conformations and provides useful implementation details, neighborhood-size analysis, and quantitative evidence of molecular neighborhood purity.
weaknesses: The partial-symmetry claim conflicts with the stated architecture. If two inputs differ exactly by a rotation, their invariant embeddings and invariant offset predictions must coincide, and the proposed canonicalization maps them to the same output. Consequently, RECON cannot distinguish rotation-equivalent 6/9 inputs through contextual orientation as claimed in Section 5.1 and Appendix D.2. Differences between actual handwritten shapes may explain the examples, but do not establish the claimed capability.

Proposition 3.1 lacks explicit assumptions needed by its proof. Appendix B invokes a right-invariant metric and local convexity conditions for stability of the Fréchet mean without establishing that the relevant distributions satisfy them. The general Lie-group statement and broad or multimodal distributions require more careful treatment.

The implemented estimators do not generally match the theoretical geodesic Fréchet mean. Appendices C and E equate it with the circular mean on SO(2) and an SVD-based matrix-Fisher mode on SO(3); these are generally different estimators. The claimed consistency and canonical-pose independence of the Tukey extension are also unsupported: symmetric multimodal distributions admit multiple equivalent minima, and fixed initialization does not guarantee translation-equivariant mode selection.

Comparisons are insufficient to establish competitiveness. SGM, the closest symmetry-discovery method, receives qualitative comparisons but no quantitative distribution-recovery or downstream evaluation. There are also no comparisons with simple geometric alignment or test-time rotation averaging. Frame averaging can enforce invariance at inference without retraining, although accuracy may suffer, so the stated practical distinction is overstated.

The molecular evaluation uses reference-aligned conformers with three synthetically assigned rotation distributions and splits conformers within each molecular identity. This establishes recovery of imposed augmentation patterns for known molecules, rather than discovery of naturally occurring orientation distributions or generalization to unseen molecular identities. The downstream improvement is modest, from 52.40% to 55.70%, against 97.01% with augmentation reversal.

The OOD implementation does not faithfully evaluate the advertised likelihood score. MNIST uses absolute angular deviation without accounting for class-dependent support widths; FashionMNIST refers to unspecified symmetry ranges despite Gaussian training distributions; and the molecular score omits the parameter-dependent density normalizer. These choices need clarification and controlled evaluation.

Experiments use a single fixed seed, lack uncertainty across runs, and assess molecular recovery primarily through parameter MSE with a visually chosen accuracy threshold. Distribution-level metrics, stronger estimator ablations, and evaluation across decomposition backbones are needed to support the robustness and architecture-agnostic claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a practical problem with class-pose decompositions: arbitrary canonical orientations can produce distribution shifts for frozen downstream models. The proposed normalization is simple and potentially useful.

The reported image canonicalization gains are substantial: MNIST accuracy increases from 66.90% to 92.94%, and FashionMNIST from 57.52% to 80.32%. OOD detection also improves over the implemented IE-AE baseline.

The SO(3) experiments extend evaluation beyond images. The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, a neighborhood-size ablation, and evidence that molecular neighborhoods preserve identity well (average hit rate 0.95).
weaknesses: The central guarantee is insufficiently qualified. Proposition 3.1 states a result for general Lie groups, but its proof requires a right-invariant metric and invokes local convexity and Lipschitz stability of the Fréchet mean without establishing the necessary support conditions. The broad and multimodal distributions discussed elsewhere are not covered by that argument. The theorem also does not establish consistency for the implemented fixed-k neighborhood estimator.

The implementation does not consistently compute the mathematical quantity analyzed. Appendices C and E identify the circular mean on SO(2), and an SVD-derived matrix-Fisher mode on SO(3), with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean; these are generally different estimators. Appendix E.2.4 also describes matrix-Fisher moment matching through the scalar function coth(s)−1/s without deriving its applicability to the general SO(3) model. These discrepancies undermine the connection between the proof and experiments.

The robust extension does not resolve canonical ambiguity as claimed. Equal, separated modes can yield multiple Tukey-loss minimizers. Initializing optimization at a common group element does not establish a unique, translation-equivariant selection, so consistency across arbitrary canonical frames remains unproven. Figure 8 provides illustrations, but no downstream ablation demonstrates this extension's benefits.

The claim that RECON distinguishes classes related by a group transformation conflicts with its invariance assumptions. If two inputs are exactly rotation-related, their invariant embeddings and invariant offset predictions coincide, and the proposed canonicalization maps them to the same result. Actual handwritten 6s and 9s can differ structurally, but Figure 5b does not establish the claimed ability to recover orientation-dependent distinctions lost by invariant representations.

Comparative evaluation is too limited for the claimed contribution. SGM, identified as the closest method, receives qualitative rather than quantitative comparisons. The downstream experiments mainly compare against no canonicalization and arbitrary IE-AE canonicalization, whose mismatch with an upright-trained classifier is expected. Simple data-aligned registration, alternative centering methods, and test-time rotation averaging would provide more informative comparisons. Architecture-agnostic compatibility is not tested across multiple decomposition backbones.

The 3D evidence supports a narrower conclusion than discovery of real-world intrinsic symmetries. Conformers are first aligned using molecular identity and then assigned one of three synthetic rotation distributions; train and test contain the same molecular identities. This evaluates recovery of imposed distributions on unseen conformers, not generalization to unseen molecules or naturally occurring orientation distributions. The MSE<800 criterion for accurate recovery is justified visually, and molecular classification improves only from 52.40% to 55.70%, far below the 97.01% augmentation-reversed reference.

The OOD evaluation has material specification problems. Appendix F replaces the claimed likelihood score with angular deviation for images, ignoring predicted distribution width; its proposed surrogate scores are not equivalent up to a within-support constant. FashionMNIST uses Gaussian rotations but does not specify the finite ID/OOD boundaries. Molecular scores omit the parameter-dependent normalization constant, which can affect rankings across inputs. Together with single-seed evaluation and absent uncertainty estimates, these issues weaken the evidence for reliable improvements.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: arbitrary canonical orientations can make learned pose distributions difficult to compare and can degrade frozen downstream models. The proposed normalization is simple and modular.
The image canonicalization results are promising: MNIST accuracy improves from 66.90% to 92.94%, and FashionMNIST from 57.52% to 80.32%, without retraining the downstream classifiers.

The SO(3) experiments extend the empirical scope beyond images. The molecular neighborhood analysis, including a mean same-molecule hit rate of 0.95, provides useful evidence for the latent-neighbor approximation.

The appendix provides substantial architecture, preprocessing, and training details, and the paper acknowledges limitations involving backgrounds, multiple objects, and predefined transformation groups.
weaknesses: The main theoretical guarantee and implementation are insufficiently aligned. Proposition 3.1 omits the right-invariant metric and concentration conditions invoked by its proof to establish equivariance and stability of the Fréchet mean. Appendices C and E also incorrectly identify the circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean in general; similarly, the SO(3) SVD/matrix-Fisher mode estimator is not generally that intrinsic mean. Consequently, the proposition does not directly justify the implemented estimators.

The claimed ability to distinguish classes related by an exact group transformation conflicts with the method's invariance assumptions (Section 5.1 and Appendix D.2). If y = ρ(h)x, invariant embeddings give identical neighborhoods and invariant Λ predictions, while equivariant ψ implies C(y) = C(x). Thus RECON cannot preserve a distinction based solely on orientation while granting full group invariance. The observed separation of handwritten 6s and 9s may exploit shape differences or approximate equivariance, but does not establish the claimed resolution of partial symmetries.

The robust multimodal extension lacks the guarantees asserted in the main text. Equal, separated modes can produce multiple Tukey-objective minimizers. A common initialization does not establish consistent, reference-frame-equivariant mode selection, and may undermine independence from arbitrary canonicals. Evidence consists of illustrative SO(2) simulations rather than downstream ablations demonstrating robust performance.

Comparisons are too limited to establish competitiveness. Most quantitative comparisons are against raw inputs or unnormalized IE-AE, whose arbitrary orientation is predictably unfavorable for a classifier trained on upright inputs. SGM receives qualitative comparisons, but there are no quantitative comparisons with stronger canonicalization alternatives, simple geometric alignment, or test-time rotation averaging. Architecture independence is also not demonstrated across multiple decomposition backbones.

The evaluation supports a narrower claim than discovery of realistic instance-specific symmetries. All target pose distributions are synthetically imposed. Molecular conformers are first aligned to a reference and filtered, and train/test splits share molecular identities; only three assigned distribution templates are used. This tests recovery of controlled augmentation distributions for known molecule classes, rather than generalization to unseen molecules or naturally occurring orientation distributions. The molecular classification gain is modest, 52.40% to 55.70%, versus 97.01% with augmentation reversed.

The OOD evaluation does not faithfully implement the advertised likelihood score. Appendix F uses absolute angular deviation for images, ignoring predicted distribution width; this is not equivalent to uniform negative log likelihood. FashionMNIST's ID/OOD thresholds are unspecified despite Gaussian training distributions having no finite support boundary. The molecular score omits the matrix-Fisher normalizer, which can vary across predicted parameters and affect pooled rankings. These issues weaken the interpretation and reproducibility of the reported AUC improvements.

Experimental uncertainty and distribution-recovery quality are insufficiently characterized. Runs use one fixed seed, without variability across training runs. The molecular claim that roughly 80% of predictions are accurate uses a visually selected parameter-MSE threshold rather than a calibrated distributional metric or comparative baseline. These evaluation gaps, together with the theoretical inconsistencies, outweigh the encouraging image results at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful limitation of class-pose representations: arbitrary canonical orientations can obscure pose distributions and degrade frozen downstream models. Explicitly estimating and removing this offset is simple and practically motivated.

Reports substantial improvements over unprocessed inputs: classification accuracy increases from 65.11% to 90.96% on MNIST and from 57.14% to 81.96% on FashionMNIST. OOD detection also improves over the uncentered IE-AE baseline across all three datasets.
Includes both SO(2) image experiments and SO(3) molecular experiments, alongside useful neighborhood-size ablations, neighbor-purity measurements, failure examples, and computational details.

Training the canonicalizer independently of the downstream classifier is an attractive feature, and the manuscript discusses important limitations involving background clutter and overlapping latent classes.
weaknesses: The theoretical result does not adequately cover the claimed setting. Proposition 3.1 is stated for general Lie groups, but its proof requires a right-invariant metric and invokes local convexity and Lipschitz stability of the Fréchet mean without establishing the required support conditions. Moreover, the consistency argument assumes independent samples from a true class, whereas the implementation uses small, learned k-nearest-neighbor sets; no guarantee connects these procedures.

The implemented estimators differ from the mathematical definitions. Appendices C and E equate the circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean on SO(2), and use SVD-based averaging or a fitted distribution's mode as the SO(3) Fréchet mean. These are not generally equivalent. Appendix E.2.4 also describes estimating general matrix-Fisher concentrations by independently inverting coth(s) - 1/s, which is not the general SO(3) matrix-Fisher moment equation. These discrepancies undermine the connection between the theorem and the reported symmetry estimates.

The Tukey-Fréchet extension does not resolve canonical ambiguity as claimed. Equally weighted, separated modes can yield multiple equally valid minimizers. Initializing optimization at a common coordinate does not establish consistent, reference-frame-independent mode selection. The appendix provides illustrative simulations but no end-to-end robustness ablation or justification for treating this estimator as a drop-in replacement in the theory.

The claimed ability to distinguish classes related by a group transformation conflicts with the stated invariance assumptions. If y = gx, invariant embeddings and invariant Λ predictions coincide, and the proposed canonicalizer satisfies C(y) = C(x). Thus it cannot preserve distinct canonical identities for exact rotated copies. The handwritten 6/9 examples may exploit shape differences, but they do not demonstrate the claimed resolution of this fundamental ambiguity.

The molecular evaluation provides limited evidence of generalizable symmetry discovery. Rotation distributions are artificially assigned from only three parameter matrices, and conformers of every molecule appear across training and test splits. This evaluates new conformers of known molecular identities rather than unseen molecules or naturally occurring pose distributions. Furthermore, calling MSE below 800 accurate is poorly calibrated: a constant predictor equal to the average of the three ground-truth matrices obtains approximately 741 entrywise MSE for every class. Distributional metrics and simple constant/oracle baselines are needed.

The evaluation protocol has material weaknesses. Appendix F.2 explicitly selects EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters using test accuracy. The image OOD implementation uses absolute angular deviation rather than the advertised distribution likelihood, ignoring predicted class-dependent spread; the FashionMNIST Gaussian ID/OOD boundary is also insufficiently specified. Consequently, the reported AUC improvements do not cleanly validate recovery of calibrated pose distributions.

The contribution is primarily a centering procedure built on existing class-pose models, yet quantitative symmetry-recovery comparisons with the closest method, SGM, are missing, and compatibility with other decomposition backbones is not demonstrated. Downstream evidence remains confined to two small image benchmarks and a constructed molecular task, where accuracy improves only from 52.40% to 55.92%. These results are useful, but insufficient to offset the unresolved technical and evaluation issues at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: arbitrary canonical orientations can make otherwise useful class-pose representations unsuitable for frozen downstream models. The proposed centering correction is simple and interpretable.

Reports meaningful improvements over uncorrected canonicalization and frozen classifiers. FashionMNIST accuracy increases from 57.14% to 81.96%, and reported OOD detection improves across all three datasets.

Includes SO(2) and SO(3) experiments, implementation details, neighborhood-size analyses, neighborhood-purity measurements, and computational costs. These provide useful evidence beyond qualitative canonicalization examples.
weaknesses: The central guarantee is broader than its justification. Proposition 3.1 states a result for general Lie groups, but Appendix B relies on a right-invariant metric and local geometric conditions supporting uniqueness and stability of the Fréchet mean without incorporating these conditions into the proposition. The broad, nearly ring-shaped SO(3) distributions used experimentally are not shown to satisfy the invoked concentration conditions. Nontrivial stabilizers also preclude a globally equivariant, single-valued group-pose estimator; Appendix D.1 acknowledges ambiguity but does not resolve its implications for the theorem.

The implementation does not consistently compute the estimator analyzed theoretically. Appendices C and E.1 equate the circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean, which is false in general. Appendix E.2 instead estimates an SO(3) centroid using a fitted matrix-Fisher mode, without establishing equivalence to the stated intrinsic mean. Its scalar concentration inversion also needs justification for general matrix-Fisher estimation. These discrepancies undermine the connection between the proof and experiments.

The claimed ability to distinguish rotation-related classes is not justified by the architecture. For exactly rotation-related inputs, invariant embeddings and invariant offset predictors must coincide, and the proposed canonicalizer produces identical outputs. Thus separate normalization cannot recover the distinction between exact rotated copies of a '6' and '9'. Success on handwritten examples may exploit shape differences or approximate invariance, but does not establish the claimed solution to partial symmetry.

The robust extension does not establish canonical-independent mode selection. Symmetric multimodal distributions can have several equally optimal Tukey-Fréchet centroids. Initializing optimization at a common group element, as suggested in Appendix C, does not guarantee that the selected mode transforms appropriately when the arbitrary canonical changes. The assertion of consistent mode selection therefore needs qualification, and the extension lacks downstream ablations.

The evaluation supports a narrower claim than general instance-specific symmetry discovery. Every benchmark uses artificially imposed rotations; GEOM conformers are first aligned using molecular identities, and train/test splits share the same molecules with randomly assigned distribution types. This tests recovery on new conformers of known identities, not generalization to unseen molecules or discovery of naturally occurring pose distributions. There is no quantitative symmetry-recovery comparison with SGM or other competitive estimators, and the molecular MSE threshold deemed 'accurate' is justified mainly through visualization.

The OOD implementation does not match the advertised likelihood score. Appendix F.1 uses absolute angular deviation for images, ignoring predicted distribution widths. This is not equivalent to uniform negative log likelihood, nor do the two proposed surrogates differ only by a within-support constant. FashionMNIST uses Gaussian rotations but its ID/OOD 'ranges' are not defined. For molecules, dropping the predicted matrix-Fisher normalization constant can affect rankings across inputs. Consequently, the AUC results do not cleanly validate Equation 5.

Experimental controls and reporting need improvement. Appendix F.2 explicitly selects baseline hyperparameters using test accuracy. The main comparisons do not establish matched access to rotated unlabeled training data or comparable training budgets, and straightforward frozen-model rotation-averaging baselines are absent. The molecular canonicalization gain is modest—52.40% to 55.92%, versus 96.40% with augmentation reversal—so broad claims about restoring pretrained performance are overstated. Overall, the useful empirical gains do not outweigh the unresolved technical and evaluation issues.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: arbitrary canonical orientations can create distribution shifts when canonicalization is applied to frozen predictors. Separating pose estimation from data-dependent orientation normalization is a clear and practical idea.

The reported improvements over unprocessed inputs are substantial on MNIST and FashionMNIST: accuracy increases from 65.11% to 90.96% and from 57.14% to 81.96%, respectively. RECON also exceeds the reported EquiAdapt results on FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 without using class labels for canonicalizer training.

Evaluation includes both SO(2) images and SO(3) molecular conformations. The appendix provides useful neighborhood-size ablations, neighborhood-purity measurements, failure examples, architecture descriptions, and computational information.
weaknesses: The claimed ability to distinguish classes related by a group transformation conflicts with the stated invariance guarantees (Section 5.1 and Appendix D.4). If y = gx, invariant embeddings give identical neighborhoods and invariant Λ gives Λ(y) = Λ(x). Together with equivariant ψ, this implies C(y) = C(x). RECON therefore cannot preserve distinct canonical identities for genuinely rotation-equivalent 6/9 instances. Differences between handwritten shapes or approximate equivariance could explain the examples, but they do not establish the claimed resolution of partial symmetries.

The theoretical guarantee is broader than its justification. Proposition 3.1 does not explicitly state the right-invariant metric and support/convexity conditions used in Appendix B to establish stability of the Fréchet mean. Broad or multimodal distributions need not satisfy those conditions. The Tukey extension does not resolve this generally: equally weighted symmetric modes can have multiple minimizers, and initialization at a fixed starting point does not guarantee right-translation-equivariant mode selection. Consequently, canonical-reference independence is not established for an important advertised regime.

The implemented estimators do not consistently match the mathematical definitions. Appendices C and E equate the circular mean with the intrinsic squared-geodesic Fréchet mean on SO(2), although these differ in general. Likewise, an SVD-based SO(3) mean is generally an extrinsic mean, rather than the intrinsic mean used in the theorem. Appendix E.2.4 also describes matrix-Fisher parameter estimation through the scalar inverse-Langevin equation, without justifying its applicability to the general matrix-Fisher normalizer. These discrepancies undermine the connection between the proof and empirical distribution estimates.

Evidence for distribution recovery lacks strong quantitative comparisons. SGM, identified as the closest instance-level distribution-learning method, is compared qualitatively but not through distribution-recovery metrics. Molecular experiments use only three synthetic parameter matrices, with the same molecular identities present across training and testing. The claim that approximately 80% of molecules are accurately recovered uses an MSE threshold selected from visualizations, without a calibrated distributional metric or simple constant-parameter baseline. This does not establish broad instance-specific recovery or generalization to unseen molecular identities.

The OOD implementation differs materially from the likelihood-based method advertised in Equation 5. For images, Appendix F uses absolute angular deviation, ignoring the predicted class-dependent distribution width; this is not equivalent to uniform negative log likelihood and does not test the benefit of recovering the full distribution. FashionMNIST uses Gaussian augmentations, but its supposedly class-specific ID/OOD ranges are not defined. For molecules, omitting the parameter-dependent normalizing constant can change rankings across examples with different predicted distributions.

The evaluation protocol explicitly selects EquiAdapt and ESCNN hyperparameters using test accuracy (Appendix F.2), compromising the independence of the reported comparisons. Moreover, RECON learns from rotated training data while the reference equivariant classifiers are trained on unrotated data, so these comparisons do not isolate architectural or canonicalization benefits under matched data access.

The breadth of the practical claims exceeds the evidence. Only one class-pose backbone family is evaluated, with small image benchmarks and artificially rotated, prealigned molecules. Molecular canonicalization improves accuracy only from 52.40% to 55.92%, far below the 96.40% augmentation-reversed reference. The frozen-backbone benefit is real, but requires substantial separate training—approximately 7.5 GPU-days for the molecular pipeline—and has not been demonstrated on large pretrained models or naturally occurring pose shifts.
